tagline.text: A small war memorial park in Puerto Princesa on the site of the Palawan Massacre

children.text: Plaza Cuartel is a memorial park built on the site of the Palawan Massacre, where on December 14, 1944, late in World War II, Japanese soldiers trapped 150 American prisoners of war in air-raid shelters and set them on fire. It is small, but it is one of the few historic sites in Puerto Princesa, admission is free, and it pairs well with the neighboring cathedral.

Plaza Cuartel is a small historic park on Taft Street in the center of Puerto Princesa. It stands on the site of the old Philippine Constabulary barracks, which during World War II served as "Palawan Prisoner of War Camp 10A," where the Japanese held American prisoners. Today it is a war memorial park with a restored arched entrance, a memorial marker and the remains of ruined buildings. It sits across a street from the Immaculate Conception Cathedral, so city tours almost always stop at both. It is not a place to linger long, but it reminds you that Puerto Princesa is not just the gateway to the underground river but a city that lived through the pain of war.

The site is in the history books because of the Palawan Massacre of December 14, 1944. On August 12, 1942, about 300 American soldiers captured in the battles of Bataan and Corregidor were brought to Puerto Princesa and confined in these barracks. For about two years they were forced to clear an airfield and build aircraft revetments using only hand tools and wheelbarrows. The concrete runway they laid by hand is described as about 1,530 yards (about 1.4 km) long and about 75 yards wide, and they also built revetments for 150 Japanese planes. The prisoners suffered beatings and hunger and survived on about one mess kit of rice a day, and of four escape attempts, two are known to have succeeded in August 1942. On September 22, 1944, half of the prisoners were sent back to Manila, and when Allied bombing began in October 1944, the remaining men dug air-raid shelters. Then on December 14, when the air-raid warning sounded, 150 prisoners went into the shelters, and the Japanese soldiers poured gasoline at the entrances and set them alight. Those who got out of the flames were shot. 139 men were killed and 11 survived and reached Allied lines.

What happened after the massacre also changes how you see this park. When the US Eighth Army landed on Palawan on February 28, 1945, some of those in charge of the camp were killed in the fighting or went missing, and the victims' bones were discovered early that year. After the war, General Tomoyuki Yamashita was hanged on February 23, 1946 under command responsibility, and in the war crimes trials 33 people were charged and 16 were tried, with verdicts on November 8, 1948. The victims' remains are said to have been taken to the United States and buried at Jefferson Barracks National Cemetery in Missouri. That is why today Plaza Cuartel has not graves but a memorial marker, ruins and people who come to remember that day. Among the survivors, Glenn McDole and Rufus Willie Smith left accounts later, and McDole's story became the book Last Man Out. The opening scenes of the 2005 film The Great Raid also depict this event. The 11 survivors escaped to southern Palawan with the help of Philippine Scouts and guerrillas under Nazario Mayor, and a US Navy PBY Catalina picked them up at Brooke's Point and flew them to Morotai.

For travelers, it is free to enter and in the city center, so it is easy to fit into a city tour. Some reviews say the site is not well maintained, and a visit is short. This guide therefore recommends walking it together with nearby city sights such as the Immaculate Conception Cathedral, the Baywalk and the Palawan Museum rather than making a separate trip just for Plaza Cuartel. This is not a place for taking photos as a tourist attraction but a place that honors the victims. Please watch your words and behavior, and pause for a moment in front of the memorial marker. Exhibits and opening conditions can change, so it is a good idea to check the latest notices before you go.
The arched entrance that preserves a trace of the barracks gives the park its first impression. You can feel that it was the gateway of the old barracks, and past it the ruins and lawn continue.
A memorial marker stands in honor of the prisoners who died. The marker is described as bearing the names and dates of the victims. Take time to read the date, December 14, 1944, and the names.

Remains of walls and building foundations let you imagine the scale and layout of the barracks at the time. The shelters the prisoners dug were divided into A (about 50 men), B (about 35) and C (up to about 30), each said to have a hidden exit toward the cliff.

This Neo-Gothic cathedral is right next to Plaza Cuartel. Seeing the present building, completed in 1961, together with the history of the first Mass in 1872 lets you read the story of Puerto Princesa at a glance.

blocks.title: Palawan Special Battalion WWII Memorial Museum

children.text: A separate museum on the Rizal Avenue side, with an admission fee listed at ₱30 by the tourism office but at ₱50 in more recent travel guides, so budget about
. It is said to display old military vehicles, guns and ammunition, American soldiers' uniforms, wartime banknotes and a wall with the names of about 1,000 Special Battalion guerrillas.

This park is a starting point for understanding Palawan's war in 1942–1945. Seen together with the story of how the superintendent of nearby Iwahig Prison secretly helped the guerrillas, the war history of this area takes on more depth.

items.title: City walking course
items.subtitle: Plaza Cuartel, the cathedral and the Baywalk

children.text: Have breakfast at your hotel in the city and head to Plaza Cuartel. It is easy walking before the sun gets high.
Quietly look around the arched entrance, the memorial marker and the barracks site. Including time to read the signs,
20~30 minutes
is enough.
Move to the Immaculate Conception Cathedral right next door and see the interior and exterior.
Walk toward the Baywalk to rest by the sea, or have an early lunch at a restaurant in the city.
Because it is a memorial park, avoid loud talking and playful photos. There is little shade at midday when the sun is strong, so morning or late afternoon is recommended.
Look around Plaza Cuartel and the cathedral.
Go to the Palawan Special Battalion WWII Memorial Museum and see the exhibits.
Have lunch and rest in the city.
Go to the Iwahig Prison and Penal Farm and see the information center and the handicraft shop.
Most Puerto Princesa city tours bundle these places. Prices and inclusions differ by operator.
Flights run from Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL) in Manila to Puerto Princesa International Airport (PPS), and the flight takes about
1 hour 30 minutes
or so.
Flights and fares vary by season, so check the airline's app a few weeks before departure.

items.title: From the airport to the city

children.text: Wikivoyage (as of March 2025) and a transport guide updated in May 2026 list a tricycle from the airport to the city at about
, a jeepney at about ₱10~25 (boarded on the highway in front of the airport), and a taxi from about ₱200 to resorts at up to ₱350.
The airport is not far from the city, so it works well to go straight to your hotel on arrival and then explore on foot.
Plaza Cuartel is right beside the Immaculate Conception Cathedral on Taft Street, so you can even walk there from hotels in the city center.
A blog report says a shared tricycle ride costs about ₱8 per person and a private ride costs about ₱50 per trip. It is said to take about
15~20 minutes
from your accommodation.
A city jeepney ride is usually listed at about ₱10 per person.
Fares vary with the season and bargaining, so confirm before you ride.
Plaza Cuartel is an outdoor park with little shade, so the dry season from December to May is comfortable. In Puerto Princesa the dry season is roughly this period.

During the day, morning or late afternoon when the sun is low is best. December 14 is the anniversary of the Palawan Massacre, so memorial events may be held around that date. If you plan around it, check local notices.

The area around Plaza Cuartel is the old center of Puerto Princesa, with many hotels and restaurants along Rizal Avenue and the Baywalk. You can walk to this park, the cathedral and the seaside promenade, so staying in the city center makes getting around easy. When booking, it helps to plan your city tour and underground river tour together.

In the city you can easily find Palawan seafood restaurants and Filipino local eateries. There is no restaurant inside the park, so a morning visit followed by lunch in the city works well. Business names and opening hours change often, so check on a map app.
Admission is free, but it is a memorial park, so watch your words and behavior.
There is little shade, so bring a hat, sunscreen and water.
A visit takes 20 to 30 minutes, so combine it on foot with the cathedral, the Baywalk and the museum.
It honors the victims, so avoid playful photos in front of the memorial marker.
The WWII museum on Rizal Avenue has a separate admission fee (about ₱30~50), so bring cash.
Blog reviews say the park's upkeep is disappointing, so go with the mindset of seeing history rather than high expectations.
Opening hours are not clearly announced, so visit during the daytime.
The city has few crosswalks and cars rarely yield, so be careful when crossing the street.
This is a memorial park honoring war victims. Do not talk loudly or climb on the memorial marker.
The number of victims differs by source. Wikipedia lists 139 dead and 11 survivors, but another guide also says 143.
Reviews say the upkeep is poor, so do not expect large facilities.
Check locally for exact opening hours and any construction.
Traffic in the city is heavy and consideration for pedestrians is low, so take care crossing the road.
Museum fees and hours can change.
The central city of Palawan, where Plaza Cuartel stands, has a cathedral, museums, the Baywalk and restaurant streets. From the park you can walk to many places in the city.
Known as a UNESCO World Heritage site, it is Palawan's signature sight. It is away from the city, so it is usually booked as a separate day.
An island-hopping area north of Puerto Princesa, good for spending a day at sea apart from the city tour.
Known as an archaeological site, it is far to the south, so it is a separate trip.
